reason: The court used this hypothetical issue-answering point while explaining paper title and prescription, but the extracted statement omits the necessary qualification that a finding of prescription would also have to be recorded.
The dates are accurately reported, but they are case facts rather than a legal holding.

The court held only that this partition action was alive solely for partitioning the corpus after rights were finally disposed of, not a broad rule that courts may keep suits alive for any specific purpose.
The quote says this defendant's notice of appeal was rejected and does not support a rule that a notice of appeal must be filed by a defendant-appellant.
The actual proposition was limited to procedural lapses causing no prejudice or harm, and it was not specifically a construction of section 35(1).
The court held that these two claims could be joined with leave under section 35(1) to avoid multiplicity and without prejudice, not that any two claims can be tried together.
The statement is broader than the holding, which concerned leave under section 35(1) for the two pleaded claims in an immovable-property action.
The failure to protest and acceptance of rent were the landlord's conduct, not the tenant's, so the statement reverses the relevant party.
The court said it was open to the landlord to terminate the tenancy but she did not do so; the extracted statement incorrectly refers to a tenant and is garbled.
The court held that the landlord's knowing acceptance of the subletting and continued rent acceptance amounted to waiver or condonation barring ejectment for subletting.
The court decided that Nandawathi's rights devolved on her husband and minor children on these facts, not a general rule for every deceased person's mortgage rights.
The court expressly treated the protection under sections 13 and 14 as statutory protection that could not be taken away.
The court held that prescription was suspended until the minor children's disability was removed by majority or death.
The true holding was limited to authority to act as a recognized agent under Civil Procedure Code section 25(b), not the general validity of all powers of attorney.
Because the plaint caption showed the plaintiff resident within the local limits while suing through an attorney, the court upheld the direction to amend the defective caption.
The classification of arbitration clauses was background law taken from prior authority, while this court's operative holding concerned the particular lease clause.
The statement describes one category from prior arbitration authority but was not itself the holding of this case.
The court's point depended on the Arbitration Act commencing after the lease and guarantee were executed, a material temporal qualification omitted from the statement.
The holding concerned motor-vehicle registration only, so the unqualified statement about registration generally is unsafe.
The court adopted and applied the rule that motor-vehicle registration deems ownership only for registration-related duties, not real ownership.
The court applied section 736 to hold that an estate-property contest involving the accounting party belongs in the judicial-settlement proceeding.
The rule was confined to belated joinder or misjoinder objections under section 22, not all objections at any late stage of trial.
The court relied on the rule that misjoinder objections must be taken before the hearing and treated the late objection as waived.
Although the court used broad language, the safe holding is qualified by the added party's interest and necessity for effectual determination of the issues.
The court decided only that calling the notary and attesting witness was sufficient on these facts, not a general rule that the best possible evidence should be presented.
